title: n says /n/
parentNote: Today is /n/, and it is the twin of /m/: both come out of your nose rather than your mouth. Pinch your child's nose gently while they hum /n/ and the sound stops — that is the quickest way to show what the two have in common and why they get muddled. The other thing to watch for is /n/ in the middle of a word: "sand" often comes out as "sad" because the /n/ is short and easy to skip. Slow those words right down and let them feel their tongue go up before the last sound.

activities.mouthCue: Tongue up behind your top teeth, and hum. The sound comes out of your nose — pinch it and /n/ disappears.
activities.prompt: You can hold this one as long as you like, just like /m/.
Both of these come down your nose. /m/ has your lips shut; for /n/ they stay open. Which is /n/?
Your tongue is in the same spot for /n/ and /d/. One you can hold, one is a tap.
Two sounds, vowel first. Stretch the second one: aaa-nnn.
Now /n/ starts the word. To nag is to keep on and on asking.
Small vowel in the middle. A fin is the flap a fish steers with.
Careful — both of these sounds live in your nose. Keep them separate.
Five sounds, the longest word yet. Take them one at a time and don't drop the /n/.
A small word you will use in nearly every sentence from now on.
Same first sound, same last sound. Only the middle tells you which.
Three that start the same. Listen to the very end.
One of these has an extra sound hiding before the last one.
The last sound decides it. Does it buzz or not?

activities.label: Words from earlier days
activities.prompt: No /n/ in any of these. Read them the way you did before.
